results.title: Bruce Archer paper 'An introduction to design research'
results.text: These considerations apply to any kind of research. Most design research, however, indeed most research, is neither objective nor scientific, neither academic nor grant-aided. It is the sort of research which is sometimes called Action research. It begins with a problem which demands inform­ ation or ideas. The search may on occasion be for information which is not new, by means which are not replicable and on grounds based in valuejudgement. Insofar as it allows decisions to be made or action to be taken, it suffices. This is mainly research for the purposes of design, and it mostly falls into the class of design information. It is mainly undertaken by designers, or by specialists for the benefit of designers, in the course of ordinary design projects. Research into design embraces the study of design activity, design sensibility and the design scene. It is undertaken by design researchers for the ultimate benefit of design practitioners, managers, teachers and so on. In order to earn its support, usually grantaided, it must generally take an academic or scholarly form. results.title: Job 170 | Design analysis project, report number 108.1
results.text: This project has sought to probe fairly deeply into the nature of architect­ ural design processes. To do this it has imported and adopted methods and tools from other sciences. In particular it has developed a new observation analysis methodology based on the repertory grid method of eliciting subjective constructs and the computational technique of multi-dimensional scaling for inferring structure from grid data. It has also used the computer as a modelling medium to express theories a) about the nature of individual design processes and b) about the nature of organisational design practice. These techniques and models have been brought to a stage of development where several applications can be seen. In particular the organisational moded 'SHADO' has potential as a project management aid as well as an aid to the evaluation of computer applications in terms of org­ anisational performance. The other model, SIMDAC, gives rise to the possibility of "intelligent" design aids. Also both models and measurement techniques have educational implications (c.f. Chapter 5.4).
